title: Influence before the decision window closes—not after the answer is polished
goal: Sequence cross-organization involvement early while labeling evidence, unknowns, and commitments honestly.
tag: Distinguished Engineer · cross-org influence · decision timing
concept:
If friends must choose a restaurant by noon, sending a perfect review at 2 PM does not help. Sending “the kitchen is definitely safe” at 9 AM before checking is also harmful.

Cross-organization technical influence has the same timing problem. A Distinguished Engineer should expose the decision question early, bring in the people who own constraints, and label what is known, provisional, and still being tested. This is an influence sequence: the right evidence reaches the right decision owner before the choice becomes expensive to change.
example: A platform team investigates a managed change-data-capture service for eight weeks. Consumer roadmaps lock in week 6. Waiting until week 8 produces a polished recommendation that no team has capacity to adopt. Instead, in week 2 the DE shares the problem, current evidence, open security and replay questions, and the week-5 test. Security and two consumer owners shape the test. The week-6 decision uses the new evidence without pretending the service was proven in week 2.

use_case.when: Use an influence sequence when evidence takes time to develop but another team's budget, roadmap, security review, or vendor decision will close first.
use_case.example: A data-platform group is evaluating managed CDC while security, finance, and two consumer teams are making commitments that determine whether adoption is possible.
use_case.decision: Engage named decision owners early with a bounded question, current evidence, unknowns, and the next test. Wait for a finished answer only when the decision is local, reversible, and no external planning window will close.

practice: Switch among a late broadcast, an early overclaim, an honest early note, and a staged sequence. Predict whether the week-6 roadmap decision receives usable evidence without creating a false commitment.
boundary: This is an original local timing model, not Spotify's or Thoughtworks' influence process. It assumes one roadmap lock and four synthetic weeks. It omits trust history, power dynamics, procurement, regulatory review, calendar availability, decision rights, reversibility, and evidence quality.

questions: The CDC evidence is complete in week 8, but consumer roadmaps lock in week 6. What should the DE do in week 2?
Share the decision question, current evidence, unknowns, and next test with relevant owners
Declare the service proven so teams reserve capacity
Stay silent until every question is closed
Early involvement protects the decision window only when provisional evidence remains clearly provisional.
Why invite security and consumer owners before the week-5 test?
Their constraints can shape evidence while the test is still changeable
Relevant owners contribute constraints and cases; involvement is input, not automatic consensus or commitment.
When is a polished late recommendation acceptable?
The decision is local, reversible, and no external planning window closes
Several teams lock annual budgets before the evidence arrives
Security approval is required before any pilot
The sequence is needed when another party's decision becomes hard to change before research finishes.

visual_explanation: A four-week timeline shows the same CDC investigation under four influence sequences. Late contact misses the roadmap lock; early overclaim creates a broken promise; honest or staged involvement brings bounded evidence and relevant constraints to the decision in time.
written_questions: Which real platform decision has an evidence-ready date later than another team's decision date?
